new_groups.definition: Printings of the resolutions of Congress of 7 July 1778: 'Resolved unanimously, That the thanks of Congress be given to General Washington for the activity with which he marched from the camp at Valley Forge in pursuit of the enemy; for his distinguished exertions in forming the order of battle; and for his great good conduct in leading on the attack and gaining the important victory of Monmouth over the British grand army'. The resolutions of Congress.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Monsieur Gerard's message to Congress, July 1778: Count d'Estaing offers American armaments the protection of the French squadron, and the prizes they take
new_groups.definition: Printings of the French minister's message to Congress, published by order of Congress: 'His Excellency the Count D'Estaing, Vice-Admiral of France, commanding the King's squadron, is desirous of enabling all the armaments either public or private in the United States of North-America, to derive every possible advantage from the operations of this squadron in order to make prizes of the common enemy'; such armaments shall enjoy the protection of the squadron, and their prizes shall belong to them only. Signed Gerard. The French minister's message, as Congress published it.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Congress, 6 August 1778: the audience of the Sieur Gerard, Minister Plenipotentiary of the King of France
new_groups.definition: Printings of the proceedings of Congress of 6 August 1778: 'According to order the Honourable the Sieur Gerard being introduced to an audience by the two Members for that purpose appointed, and being seated in his chair, his Secretary delivered to the President a letter from his most Christian Majesty, which was read in the words following'; with the King's letter, the minister's address and the President's answer. The proceedings of Congress, as published.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: George Johnstone and Congress, August and September 1778: Congress's declaration, the commissioners' declaration and Mr. Johnstone's declaration
new_groups.definition: Three public declarations on one of the British commissioners, George Johnstone: Congress's declaration of 11 August 1778 that it is incompatible with the honour of Congress to hold any correspondence with him, and the two declarations of 26 August answering it, one by the other three commissioners and one by Mr. Johnstone. Contains those three groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Congress's declaration of 11 August 1778 on George Johnstone, one of the British commissioners
new_groups.definition: Printings of the declaration of Congress of 11 August 1778: 'Whereas George Johnstone, Esq. one of the British Commissioners for restoring peace in America, on the eleventh of April last, did write and send a letter to Joseph Reed, Esq. a Member of Congress'; it recites the passages of his letters and the account Mr. Reed gave of an offer made to him, and declares it incompatible with the honour of Congress to hold any manner of correspondence or intercourse with Mr. Johnstone. The New-York Gazette and the Newport Gazette print it with the commissioners' answers. Congress's own declaration; the allegations are those of Congress and of Mr. Reed's account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The declaration of the Earl of Carlisle, Sir Henry Clinton and William Eden, 26 August 1778, on Congress's declaration about their colleague
new_groups.definition: Printings of the declaration of three of the British commissioners, the Earl of Carlisle, Sir Henry Clinton and William Eden, dated New York, 26 August 1778: they 'have received a declaration of the American Congress, dated the 11th instant, which relates to a gentleman with whom they have the honour to be joined in commission'; 'they hereby think proper on their part solemnly to declare, that they had not any knowledge, either directly or indirectly, of the letter and conversation alluded to in the said Declaration until they saw them made public in the news-papers', and they go on to the treaty with France. Printed in the New York and Newport papers with the papers sent to Congress, and in the American papers after Congress's resolution of 31 August. The commissioners' own declaration.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: George Johnstone's declaration of 26 August 1778: he declines to act as a commissioner in anything that regards Congress
new_groups.definition: Printings of George Johnstone's declaration dated New York, 26 August 1778, in answer to Congress's declaration: having seen the declaration of Congress of 11 August and its resolution, 'The said George Johnstone for himself says, That he is far from considering the said resolution of the Congress as offensive to him; That he rather receives it as a mark of distinction'; he declares that 'the subscriber, George Johnstone, thinks proper to decline acting as a Commissioner, or otherwise interfering in any message, answer, agreement, negotiation, matter or thing that may regard the said Congress, which he does with so much the more pleasure as he is perfectly satisfied the business will be left in more able and sufficient hands', reserving the liberty of publishing a justification of his conduct. Mr. Johnstone's own declaration.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The King's speech to both Houses of Parliament, 3 June 1778, giving them a recess after a long session
new_groups.definition: Printings of the King's speech of 3 June 1778: 'My Lords and Gentlemen, After so long and laborious an application to the public business, I think it proper at this season of the year to give you some recess. I come at the same time to return you my particular thanks for the zeal you have shewn in supporting the honour of my crown'. The papers printed it in August from the June mail. The King's own speech.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: A letter from the Hague of 4 June 1778: American proposals for a treaty lie before the States of the United Provinces
new_groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from the Hague dated 4 June 1778, in London news: 'The proposals for a treaty between the Americans and the United Provinces now lie before the States; the answer I am told the Americans received on the delivery of them was, that the business required a very serious attention'. The New-York Gazette and the Newport Gazette print it in August; three American papers print it in November as 'a letter from Holland, dated in June'. A correspondent's letter, as the London papers gave it.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: September 1778: about forty sail of British ships appear off Bedford and land some 4,000 men
new_groups.definition: Printings of a report of September 1778 from New England: 'Last Saturday about 40 sail of British men of war and transports appeared off Bedford, at six o'clock they landed about 4000 British troops, Tories, &c. under the command of General Gray'; the papers' versions go on in different words to the rope-walks, houses, stores and shipping burned, and one adds a comment of its own ('Oh Clinton! can you expect that after such savage and cowardly conduct, that Americans will treat with Britons upon terms of reconciliation'). Printed by every paper that survives for its weeks, the New-York Gazette among them. A report at second hand.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The troops of the convention of Saratoga, August and September 1778: the commissioners' requisition and Congress's resolution
new_groups.definition: The two public papers on the troops that surrendered at Saratoga in October 1777, whose embarkation Congress had suspended in January 1778: the British commissioners' requisition of 26 August 1778 that the troops be allowed to sail, and Congress's resolution of 4 September 1778. Contains those two groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The commissioners' requisition of 26 August 1778: the troops of the convention of Saratoga to be allowed to embark for Great Britain
new_groups.definition: Printings of the requisition of the British commissioners, the Earl of Carlisle, Sir Henry Clinton and William Eden, dated New York, 26 August 1778: 'Upon a representation from the Commander in Chief of his Majesty's forces, that the troops lately serving under Lieutenant-General Burgoyne'; it requires that passports be given for transports to the harbour of Boston 'for the immediate embarkation of the said troops; and that they be allowed to depart for Great-Britain in term of the said Convention', offers 'to renew, on the part of Great-Britain, all the stipulations of the said Convention', and is sent 'to the American Congress for their direct and explicit answer'. Printed with the commissioners' other papers of 26 August. The commissioners' own requisition.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Congress, 4 September 1778: no ratification of the convention of Saratoga resting on powers 'by construction and implication', or subject to the approval of Parliament, can be accepted
new_groups.definition: Printings of the resolution of Congress of 4 September 1778: 'Whereas Congress did, on the eighth day of January, 1778, Resolve, "That the embarkation of Lieutenant General Burgoyne, and the troops under his command, be suspended till a distinct and explicit ratification of the Convention of Saratoga shall be properly notified by the Court of Great Britain to Congress"'; it resolves 'That no ratification of the Convention of Saratoga, which may be tendered in consequence of powers which may reach that case by construction and implication, or which may subject whatever is transacted relative to it to the future approbation or disapprobation of the Parliament of Great Britain, can be accepted by Congress'. Congress's answer, in effect, to the commissioners' requisition of 26 August on those troops. Printed by every paper that survives for its weeks. The resolution of Congress.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Boston, September 1778: the privateer General Hancock returns from a cruise after an engagement with the British frigate Levant
new_groups.definition: Printings of a Boston paragraph of September 1778: 'Last Monday returned into port, from a cruise, the private armed ship General Hancock, late commanded by Capt. Ishmael Hardy. On the 9th instant, she fell in with the Le Vant English frigate, of 32 guns'; it gives the course of the engagement, in which the captain of the privateer was wounded and the frigate blew up, and the privateer's boats saved part of her crew. A Boston paper's report.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Williamsburg, October 1778: intelligence that Colonel Clark has taken Fort Chartres and the other western posts between the Ohio and the Mississippi
new_groups.definition: Printings of a Williamsburg paragraph of 9 October 1778, 'Intelligence from the south-western frontiers of this state': 'Col. Clark, with a body of militia, has taken possession of Fort Charters and the other western posts between the river Ohio and Mississippi. The Commandant is on his way to this city'. A Williamsburg paper's report.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The British commissioners' manifesto and proclamation of 3 October 1778, and the manifesto of Congress of 30 October
new_groups.definition: The two manifestos of October 1778: the British commissioners' manifesto and proclamation of 3 October, addressed to the members of Congress, the assemblies and all the inhabitants, and the manifesto of Congress of 30 October. Contains those two groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The British commissioners' manifesto and proclamation of 3 October 1778, to the members of Congress, the assemblies and all the inhabitants
new_groups.definition: Printings of the manifesto and proclamation of the Earl of Carlisle, Sir Henry Clinton and William Eden, dated New York, 3 October 1778: 'To the Members of the Congress, the Members of the General Assemblies or Conventions of the several colonies, plantations and provinces' and all the free inhabitants; the commissioners say they will return to England, renew the offers made to the Congress and the assemblies, proclaim a pardon to those who return to their allegiance, and declare the manifesto in force for forty days, from 3 October to 11 November. The New-York Gazette prints it in three issues and the Newport Gazette in two; American papers print it with comments of their own. The commissioners' own manifesto.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The manifesto of Congress, 30 October 1778
new_groups.definition: Printings of the manifesto of Congress done on 30 October 1778: 'These United States, having been driven to hostilities by the oppressive and tyrannous measures of Great Britain; having been compelled to commit the essential rights of man to the decision of arms'; it declares 'That if our enemies presume to execute their threats, or persist in their present career of barbarity, we will take such exemplary vengeance as shall deter others from a like conduct'. Printed by every paper that survives for its weeks; the New-York Gazette prints it twice, the second time 'with the remarks subjoined to it'. Congress's own manifesto.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Count Pulaski to the President of Congress, 16 October 1778: his account of the enemy's attack on his men on the 15th
new_groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from General Count Pulaski to the President of Congress dated 16 October 1778: 'For fear that my first letter concerning my engagement should miscarry or be delayed, and having other particulars to mention, I thought proper to send you this letter'; it gives his account of the enemy's attack on his men on the 15th, at three o'clock in the morning, with 400 men, and of the pursuit. The commander's own report.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1778 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Boston, November 1778: the British fleet under Admiral Byron, cruising near Cape Cod, in the violent storm
new_groups.definition: Printings of a Boston paragraph of 12 November 1778: 'In the violent storm of last week, the wind being at N. E. though variable, the British fleet under the command of Admiral Byron, consisting of sixteen sail of the line, were cruising near Cape Cod'; it reports that the Somerset, of 64 guns, was cast ashore near the Race, at the head of the Cape, and entirely lost. A Boston paper's report, at second hand.

dispositions_summary.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (register Y-THIN, chosen by the owner on 23 November 2026 and amended the same night with the owner's choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks, and by at least 4; the eligible items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted (3 in 1778), and the others are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, about as many stories as a standard year (a target, not a quota); one affair's items are handled as in X-1800-01; the eligible items not chosen are listed here.
dispositions_summary.paper_counting: 1778 has 11 catalogue series, which are 8 papers (C-04): the Connecticut Courant under three catalogue numbers and the Freeman's Journal / New-Hampshire Gazette under two; the two Williamsburg Virginia Gazettes are two papers. 3 to 7 papers are in print in any three weeks, so an item needs 4 papers in almost every month (5 when its printings span weeks in which all 8 survive).

dispositions_summary.method: The automatic families first printed in 1778 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 309 items printed somewhere, 130 in 4 or more catalogue series by the finder's count), and the families of 1777 were looked for on the 1778 pages (items_from_1777.json: 36 items, one in 4 papers). Every item in 3 or more papers was compared by machine with every page (about 100 words of its text, both transcriptions); the items were joined into documents and every document that might reach the bar was counted again by about 70 words from its own opening on a reference page, with every page listed and the doubtful ones read; a sweep of passages shared word for word (seven-word sequences) by 4 or more papers found short items the families miss. 125 candidates were counted this way (outputs/story_discovery_1778/counts_1778.json). The admitted stories were searched with phrase searches over all 970 pages in both transcriptions (phrase_hits.json); every hit not in the ledger was read (recitals of the bills' titles, a second copy of the New-Jersey Gazette of 1 July, other reports naming Count d'Estaing). Each printing was checked against its page scan.

counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: Counted by their own words, 76 items of 1778 are eligible (more than half of the papers that survive for their weeks, and at least 4): 55 in 4 papers, 18 in 5, 3 in 6, none in 7. Three are printed by every paper that survives for their weeks and are admitted (the landing at Bedford, 4 of 4; Congress's resolution of 4 September, 5 of 5; the manifesto of Congress, 6 of 6). 30 more are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; the 33 items make 26 stories (21 single items and 5 parents holding the other 12 as sub-stories). 42 eligible items are not chosen; one turns on private persons and waits for the owner. 51 more candidates were counted and are below the bar.
counted_item_by_item.Joins made by the finder: The finder chains documents printed together or sharing formulas: the two draught bills and the commissioners' later papers through the bills' titles; the commissioners' declarations and requisition of 26 August through their titles; the lists of the thirteen states; standing notices of the New-York Gazette. Each text was counted by its own words.
